index.title: One page, every screen
index.desc: OxiUI draws one THTML and TCSS page in a terminal, in a browser and, later, on a microcontroller. This page runs it live in your browser.

hero.title: Write a page once. Show it in a terminal, a browser, or on a device.
hero.lead: OxiUI renders THTML (HTML-like markup) and TCSS (CSS-like styles) to SSH terminals, a browser canvas and WebAssembly running on your own machine. ESP32 screens are next.

blocks.x: The demo above is an ordinary OxiUI page. It is not a video and not a screenshot: the OxiUI core was compiled to WebAssembly, your browser downloaded it, and it lays out, paints and handles clicks locally. The same page can also be served over SSH to a real terminal.

items: **Terminal over SSH:** works today, the original target.
**Browser, server-driven:** works today (canvas client, proportional text).
**Browser, local mode:** works today and is what you see here; no server needed.
**Android shell, Linux framebuffer (OxiDE), native window:** planned or in progress, see the [roadmap](@oxiui:roadmap).
**ESP32 touch screens:** planned, after the OxiScript compiler can run programs.

how.title: How it works
how.desc: From one THTML page to a terminal, a browser or a device.
how.lead: A page is a text file. The core turns it into a display list, and a small client for each target draws that list.

items: You write a page in THTML (boxes, text, buttons, inputs) and style it with TCSS (colours, borders, flex layout, in whole character cells).
The core parses it, lays it out and produces a display list: fills, borders, paths and positioned glyph runs.
A client draws the list. A terminal client turns it into cells and escape codes, a browser client paints it on a canvas, and a device client will draw it to a screen.
Clicks and keys come back as events. Built-in actions (`inc:count`, `toggle:open`, `set:tab=a`) run in the core; anything else goes to your own App Server.

index.title: TypeScript-looking, strictly typed, compiled to WebAssembly
index.desc: OxiScript is a young, strictly typed language that reads like TypeScript and compiles to WebAssembly. Try the checker in your browser.

hero.title: A language that reads like TypeScript and is checked like Rust.
hero.lead: OxiScript is statically and soundly typed, with errors as values and mechanical fixes for common mistakes. It compiles to WebAssembly. Below, the real checker and formatter run in your browser.

items: Parser, formatter and type checker (the same code you are using above, compiled to WebAssembly).
A registry of stable error codes, each with an explanation and, often, a mechanical fix.
Host capability interfaces (`log`, `state`) that programs import with `host:` modules.
**Running programs.** Code generation exists, but the lowering step that connects the checker to it is still being built. The Run button is disabled until then.
A standard library, packages, the language server, devices. All planned, none ready.

ts.title: OxiScript for TypeScript developers
ts.desc: What stays the same, what changes, and where OxiScript is worse than TypeScript.
ts.lead: Reading OxiScript should need no learning. Writing it sometimes needs a fix. This page is honest about both.

blocks.x: The same program, nearly the same text
Only `number` became `f64`. Discriminated unions, `switch` narrowing, `const`, arrow functions and template strings are the TypeScript you know.

head: TypeScript
OxiScript
Why
rows: Integers and floats are different; overflow is defined and traps.
`a === b` only (`==` is an error with a fix)
No cast may lie about a type.

items: It cannot run programs yet. TypeScript can.
There is no npm. No ecosystem, a tiny standard library, no `async` (reserved, not built).
No `any`, no `eval`, no dynamic features. That is the point, and also a cost when porting JavaScript.
It is young. Expect rough edges and breaking changes.
